briefing.question: Who governs the university: does public funding give the state the right to shape what scholars pursue, or must the free pursuit of knowledge be shielded from whoever holds power?
briefing.split: Hamilton, executive priorities; Mill, neutrality; Aristotle, equality.

briefing.question: Progress versus stewardship: how much of the natural world and of local consent should a nation trade for growth, and who speaks for those who bear the cost?
briefing.split: Bentham and Locke would build; Burke, Leopold, Francis urge care.

briefing.question: Private virtue and public trust: how far may the state reach into private enterprise and private lives for the sake of common security?
briefing.split: Hobbes and Smith, narrow controls; Locke, only general laws.

briefing.question: Truth and tolerance: is the university a place where every claim may be heard and tested, or a community that must also protect the dignity of its members?
briefing.split: Marcuse, deny the platform; Mill, Popper, Kant, refute instead.

briefing.question: How should a free society protect a people with a long history of persecution without making some political criticism unsayable?
briefing.split: Levi and Herzl, name contempt; Milton and Mill, fear licensers.

briefing.question: Justice and complicity: when wrongdoing is tolerated by many, who bears guilt, and how do we pursue accountability without abandoning the presumption of innocence?
briefing.split: Burke, organize; Blackstone, presume innocence; Augustine, confess.

briefing.question: What is the worth of a human life when its capacities fade, and can autonomy reach across time to decide for a self that no longer remembers choosing?
briefing.agreed: Earlier and later self may differ.
briefing.split: Dworkin, precedent autonomy; Mill, Parfit, Aquinas, the present self.

briefing.question: Unity and diversity in the Church: is unity better kept by one common form or by generously making room for many legitimate traditions?
briefing.split: Cyprian, unity under bishops; Augustine, Benedict XVI, generosity.

briefing.question: The role of faith in public life: can a nation have an established Christian church that also protects every faith, or does pluralism eventually dissolve establishment?
briefing.agreed: Other faiths free; Church still teaches.
briefing.split: Hooker, Burke, establishment; Locke, Williams, separation.

briefing.question: Can a pluralist, equal citizenship be built where faith communities have long feared one another, and what do the strong owe the vulnerable?
briefing.split: Tertullian, no excuse; Washington, from within; Ashoka, respect.

briefing.question: Free speech and civic peace: may a preacher publicly criticize another faith, and when does criticism become provocation?
briefing.agreed: Criticism is no crime; threats may be stopped.
briefing.split: Mill, incitement only; Hobbes, danger; Paul, speak in love.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Blackstone speaks first because the report names his auxiliary right of having arms, the passage the modern debate keeps returning to, and because the same chapter gives the classic test for when restraint of liberty becomes tyranny. Locke follows because the report names his natural right of self-preservation and his account of what law is for. Hobbes is seated because the report names him for the opposite starting point: the sovereign's power to secure the common peace, and the liberty that exists only where the law is silent. Beccaria is seated because his chapter on false ideas of utility is the best-known Enlightenment argument against laws that forbid the carrying of arms, and he wrote it as a criminal-law reformer, not a partisan. Madison closes because he wrote of the advantage of being armed in Federalist No. 46 and drafted the amendment at issue; his own context, the militia and the balance between state and federal power, is stated plainly. Justice Thomas, the Maryland legislature and the parties are context only. Living constitutionalists and balancing-of-interests jurists named in the report are represented in the closing summary rather than seated, since the leading voices are modern and in copyright.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: when a right is fundamental, who decides where it ends, and can a right be hemmed in so tightly that it is effectively denied? The report gives one side as gun-rights supporters, who say the Court's Bruen decision promised that carry rights would be judged by history, yet states have redrawn the map so that most of daily life is a sensitive place; a right you cannot exercise on the bus, in the park or at dinner is a right in name only, and they read Justice Thomas's statement as notice that the Court will eventually say so. The other side is supporters of the Maryland law, who say crowded, enclosed or vulnerable places such as transit, hospitals, bars and places full of children are exactly where legislatures have always been allowed to limit weapons, and that elected lawmakers, not judges hunting for eighteenth-century analogues, are best placed to weigh public safety. Sir William, your Commentaries are cited on both sides. Begin.

closing.text: Where they agreed: the right to arms is real and tied to self-defense, yet legislatures may regulate it, and the real dispute is over which restrictions are necessary and which are needless. Where they split: Blackstone judges each restraint by whether it serves the public or is wanton. Locke asks whether a rule protects lives or only disarms the peaceable. Hobbes leaves the line to the lawmakers who keep the peace. Beccaria doubts that carry bans stop criminals at all. Madison holds that the right cannot be emptied but that states keep wide room to regulate.

chairs.name: William Blackstone
works: Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, ch. 1 (1765)

turn.text: Both sides quote me, and both are partly right, so let me give the whole sentence its due. The fifth auxiliary right of the subject, I wrote, is “that of having arms for their defence, suitable to their condition and degree, and such as are allowed by law.” (Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, ch. 1) I called it “a public allowance, under due restrictions, of the natural right of resistance and self-preservation, when the sanctions of society and laws are found insufficient to restrain the violence of oppression.” (Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, ch. 1) Notice the two qualifiers that travel with the right: it is suited to one's condition, and it is such as is allowed by law. I never imagined an English right to bear arms anywhere and in any manner one pleased.

turn.text: But I also gave the test by which every such law must be judged. “Political therefore, or civil, liberty, which is that of a member of society, is no other than natural liberty so far restrained by human laws (and no farther) as is necessary and expedient for the general advantage of the publick” (Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, ch. 1) And the other edge of the same blade: “every wanton and causeless restraint of the will of the subject, whether practiced by a monarch, a nobility, or a popular assembly, is a degree of tyranny.” (Commentaries on the Laws of England, Book I, ch. 1) So the question for the Maryland law is not whether the legislature may restrain the carrying of arms. That is a question of particulars, which is perhaps why the justices preferred to wait for a narrower case.

chairs.modern_read: Blackstone called the right to have arms an auxiliary right of self-defense, but one shaped by law and circumstance. He would say a legislature may restrict it where necessary for the public good, yet every needless restriction is a degree of tyranny, so each rule must be judged on its own reasons.

Adam Smith closes because his Wealth of Nations made the classic free-market exception for national defense, the exact argument behind treating chips like strategic assets. Jensen Huang, Sen. opening.text: Tonight's subject: how far may the state reach into private enterprise and private lives for the sake of common security? The report gives one side as security hawks in both parties, who say advanced chips are now as strategic as weapons, so the companies that make them, and the people who lead them, should face clearance-style scrutiny, audits and export controls; a private firm's lapse, they argue, can become a national vulnerability. The other side is skeptics, including Sen. Rand Paul, who say a personal scandal is being used to justify sweeping government control of a private industry; he said an affair alone should not cost a CEO his job and that he has not seen intelligence showing the partner was a spy, and they warn that heavy oversight could slow American innovation and hand the lead to rivals. The facts of the scandal remain disputed. Mr. Hobbes, security is your first word. Begin.

sittings.headline: Hundreds protest at Oxford as Nathan Cofnas speaks on DEI at Oriel College
sittings.question: Truth and tolerance: is the university a place where every claim may be heard and tested, or a community that must also protect the dignity of its members?

setup.text: Protesters surrounded Oriel College on Tuesday evening and tried to block its entrances as Nathan Cofnas, a self-described race realist, spoke at a Reform UK student society event titled Is DEI undermining higher education? Oriel declined to cancel, citing a statutory duty to protect free speech; many protesters invoked Prof. Jason Arday, who resigned from Cambridge and later died after Cofnas first raised plagiarism accusations against him.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: how should a free society protect a people with a long history of persecution without making some political criticism unsayable? opening.text: Tonight's subject: what is the worth of a human life when its capacities fade, and can autonomy reach across time to decide for a self that no longer remembers choosing? The report gives one side as supporters of advance requests, who say people facing dementia should be able to decide, while still competent, how their lives end rather than lose that choice as the disease advances; dignity and autonomy require it, and most also back halting the mental-illness expansion as a sensible safeguard. opening.text: Tonight's subject: is unity better kept by one common form or by generously making room for many legitimate traditions? The report gives one side as supporters, who say the Pope is guarding unity: one Roman rite around the reformed liturgy of Vatican II, and no novel experiments with the priesthood, avoids rival camps hardening into rival churches, and continuity with his predecessor is itself a stabilizing act. The other side is traditionalists, such as liturgical scholar Dom Alcuin Reid in posts circulating on X, who say the restrictions punish faithful Catholics drawn to a rite that nourished saints for centuries, and that true liturgical peace would mean generosity, as Benedict XVI's Summorum Pontificum offered; some on the reform side, meanwhile, regret the closed door on married priests. Both sides cite the Apostle: “For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ.” (1 Corinthians 12:12) Cardinal Newman, you wrote on how a tradition grows. sittings.question: The role of faith in public life: can a nation have an established Christian church that also protects every faith, or does pluralism eventually dissolve establishment?

Locke follows because the report names his Letter Concerning Toleration, the classic case that church and state are separate. Eliot is seated because the report names his Idea of a Christian Society; it is in copyright, so he is paraphrased only. Roger Williams closes because he argued, against both establishment and persecution, that civility and Christianity could flourish together among divers consciences. opening.text: Tonight's subject: can a nation have an established Christian church that also protects every faith, or does pluralism eventually dissolve establishment? The report gives one side as admirers, who say the King is describing what an established church has quietly become: a gracious host that keeps faith itself respected in public life, giving Muslims, Jews, Sikhs and others room to worship in a secularizing country; hospitality, they argue, flows from Christian conviction rather than diluting it. The other side is critics, many on X, who say the King has drifted from his coronation oath as Defender of the Faith, and that a Church whose head speaks of protecting every belief risks losing the confidence to proclaim its own; some secularists add that an established church should not be the gatekeeper of anyone's faith at all. The report sets two texts side by side, the command of hospitality, “But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.” (Leviticus 19:34) and the command of witness, “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Matthew 28:19) Master Hooker, you defended this Church. sittings.why_these_chairs: Mill speaks first because the report names his defense of offensive speech and his line between opinion and incitement. Hobbes follows because the report names the sovereign's duty to keep the peace, and Leviathan claims for the sovereign the right to judge which doctrines endanger it. Milton is seated because the report names the Milton tradition of open encounter. Locke closes because his Letter Concerning Toleration holds that religious speech and worship should be judged by the same law as any other conduct. I would say to those who think the system worked that a process which leaves a man under suspicion for seven months for words alone has already taught a whole town what not to say.

chairs.modern_read: Milton trusted truth to win in open debate, so false claims should be answered, not arrested. He would say that arresting first and deciding later acts as censorship, teaching others to stay silent.

A preacher who threatens or assaults is punished as anyone would be; a preacher who argues is protected as anyone would be.
